params.question: Which combination of symptoms in a patient with low back pain constitutes a surgical emergency requiring immediate imaging?

answers.text: Unilateral leg pain with a positive straight leg raise on one side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unilateral sciatica suggests single nerve root compression (radiculopathy), which is managed conservatively first and is not a surgical emergency.

answers.text: Morning stiffness lasting more than one hour with sacroiliac tenderness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These features suggest ankylosing spondylitis, an inflammatory condition requiring investigation but not emergency surgery.

answers.text: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This triad defines cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency where delay of even hours risks permanent incontinence and paralysis.

answers.text: Night pain with unexplained weight loss over three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Night pain and weight loss raise suspicion for spinal malignancy, which needs urgent investigation but not immediate surgical decompression.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness defines cauda equina syndrome — the one back-pain emergency where hours of delay can cause permanent damage.
Correct. Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral weakness together define cauda equina syndrome, demanding emergency MRI and surgical decompression within hours.

params.question: What is the primary initiating event in intervertebral disc degeneration that triggers the cascade leading to spondylosis?

answers.text: Hypertrophy of the facet joints from mechanical overloading

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Facet joint hypertrophy is a secondary consequence — it occurs after the disc loses height and shifts abnormal load to the posterior elements.

answers.text: Desiccation of the nucleus pulposus with loss of water-binding proteins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Declining proteoglycans cause the nucleus to lose water (from ~80% in youth to ~70% by the sixties), reducing disc height and triggering the entire degenerative cascade.

answers.text: Tears in the annulus fibrosus from repetitive flexion injuries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Annular tears are a downstream effect — they develop because the dried, flattened disc places abnormal stress on the surrounding fibrous ring.

answers.text: Osteophyte formation at the vertebral end plates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osteophytes are a late reactive bony change to altered spinal biomechanics, not the initiating event in disc degeneration.

overallFeedback.feedback: The primary event is desiccation of the nucleus pulposus. As water-binding proteins decline with age, the disc loses height and springiness, triggering secondary annular tears and facet joint arthritis.
Correct. Nucleus pulposus desiccation is the starting point — it leads to disc height loss, abnormal loading of the annulus and facet joints, and ultimately the clinical syndromes of spondylosis.

interactions.label: A patient presents with clumsy hands, spastic gait, and urinary urgency but no s

params.question: A patient presents with clumsy hands, spastic gait, and urinary urgency but no significant neck pain. Which degenerative spine syndrome best explains this presentation?

answers.text: Cervical radiculopathy due to foraminal nerve root compression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radiculopathy produces dermatomal arm pain and segmental weakness (e.g., C7 → triceps), not the upper motor neurone signs of spasticity and hand clumsiness.

answers.text: Neurogenic claudication due to lumbar spinal stenosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neurogenic claudication causes bilateral leg pain on walking relieved by forward flexion, not hand dysfunction or spastic gait.

answers.text: Cervical myelopathy due to spinal cord compression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cervical myelopathy compresses the cord itself, causing spastic gait, fine motor hand dysfunction, and urinary urgency — and is often painless early, delaying diagnosis.

answers.text: Cauda equina syndrome due to central lumbar disc herniation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cauda equina syndrome produces lower motor neurone signs (flaccid weakness, saddle anaesthesia, bladder retention), not the upper motor neurone pattern described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: This pattern — spastic gait, clumsy hands, urinary urgency without pain — points to cervical myelopathy. The spinal cord is compressed, producing upper motor neurone signs distinct from root or cauda equina compression.
Correct. Spastic gait, hand clumsiness, and urinary urgency without pain is the classic presentation of cervical myelopathy — spinal cord compression that is often painless early on.

interactions.label: Most patients with lumbar disc prolapse require surgery because herniated disc m

params.question: Most patients with lumbar disc prolapse require surgery because herniated disc material cannot be resorbed naturally by the body.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Herniated disc material is gradually resorbed by the body and nerve root inflammation settles on its own — surgery is reserved for failed conservative treatment (6–12 weeks) or emergencies like cauda equina syndrome.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The body's inflammatory response gradually resorbs herniated disc material over weeks to months, which is why most patients improve with conservative management alone.

params.question: A 58-year-old woman has bilateral leg pain on walking 300 metres, relieved by sitting and leaning forward, with normal pedal pulses. What feature most reliably distinguishes her condition from vascular claudication?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both neurogenic and vascular claudication can be painless at rest, so this does not reliably distinguish the two conditions.
Both conditions can produce bilateral symptoms, so the distribution alone is not the distinguishing feature.
Reflexes can be normal in both conditions. Normal pedal pulses help exclude vascular disease, but reflexes do not reliably differentiate the two.

answers.text: Relief of symptoms specifically with forward flexion of the spine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Positional relief with forward flexion (the 'shopping-trolley sign') is the hallmark of neurogenic claudication — flexion widens the narrowed spinal canal. Vascular claudication is relieved simply by stopping, regardless of position.

overallFeedback.feedback: The distinguishing feature is positional relief with forward flexion (the shopping-trolley sign). Neurogenic claudication eases when the spine flexes and opens the canal; vascular claudication eases just by stopping, regardless of position.

Correct. The shopping-trolley sign — relief with forward flexion — is the key distinguishing feature, because flexion opens the stenotic spinal canal. Vascular claudication eases just by stopping, in any position.
